platforms.title: It's Not a Stubborn Headache, It May Be Your Painkillers
platforms.meta_description: Taking painkillers for headaches too often can cause more headaches. How NHS advice counts risky days, why codeine and caffeine matter, and how a break works.
platforms.body_html:
You get a headache, you take two paracetamol, it eases. A day later it is back, so you take some ibuprofen. By the end of the month there are packets in your bag, your desk drawer and the bathroom cabinet, and the headaches seem more frequent than ever. It is easy to assume the headaches are simply getting worse. The NHS points to a less obvious explanation: taking painkillers for headaches too often or for a long time can itself cause headaches, known as medication overuse or rebound headaches.

How a painkiller ends up feeding the headache

Medication overuse headache develops in people who already have a headache condition, most often migraine or tension-type headache. The Birmingham Headache Centre at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust describes it in its patient leaflet (issued June 2026) as affecting approximately 2% of the world's population. According to the same leaflet, regular overuse can turn occasional headaches into a chronic daily headache, or worsen an existing one, over roughly three months.

The key measure is not how many tablets you take on a bad day but how many days a month you take anything at all. NHS inform, Scotland's national health information service, advises not taking simple painkillers such as paracetamol or anti-inflammatories on more than 15 days a month in the long term, and not taking triptans or a combination of treatments on more than 10 days a month. The Birmingham leaflet notes that the effect comes on faster with codeine or other opiate-based drugs and with triptans, appearing after only 10 days' use per month.

Some products carry more risk than others. The same leaflet advises avoiding codeine-based painkillers for headache, including shop-bought combination products, and warns that tablets containing codeine or caffeine make overuse more likely. NHS inform adds that opiates like codeine should not be prescribed for migraine at all, because they are no more effective than triptans and painkillers and can cause medication overuse headache. Painkillers you take for back or joint pain still count towards the total if you also get headaches.

3 Steps That Break the Painkiller Cycle

1. Keep a simple record for a month. NHS inform recommends keeping a record of what painkillers you take and how often. Note the date, the headache and anything you took. This turns a vague feeling into a number you can compare with the 10-day and 15-day limits, and it gives your GP exactly what they need.

2. Plan a painkiller break with your GP, not alone. The usual treatment is to stop the painkillers that are being overused. The Birmingham Headache Centre asks patients to stop all painkillers and triptans for eight weeks, unless they are on high-dose opiates, which need a supervised reduction. Headaches usually get worse before they get better, and the leaflet explains it takes around eight weeks for pain pathways in the brain to start to calm down. In its experience at least half of people get a significant improvement. A GP can help with sickness tablets, short-term sleep support or time off work during the worst weeks.

3. Use non-drug relief and ask about prevention. During the break, the leaflet suggests ice packs, heat packs, massage and regular meals, sleep and exercise, plus about two litres of non-caffeinated fluid a day. If your headaches stay frequent, ask about preventive medicine. The leaflet explains that overusing painkillers can stop preventive treatments from working, so the break also gives prevention a fairer chance.

The Three Things Worth Remembering

Looking back over the whole picture: frequent painkillers can keep a headache going; the risk is measured in days per month rather than doses; and a planned break, though tough for the first weeks, is how most people get out of the cycle. Once you are through it, the Birmingham leaflet suggests keeping any painkiller use to no more than two days a week.

The NHS advises seeing a GP if you get headaches several times a week or they are severe, or if painkillers are not helping. That is especially worth doing if your own record shows you are close to the 10-day mark, because a GP can confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes before you change anything. Call 999 for a headache that starts suddenly and is extremely painful, or that comes with numbness or weakness, sudden problems speaking, or confusion. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from your doctor.

Sources: NHS, "Tension headaches" (page reviewed August 2025) and "Headaches"; NHS inform, "Migraine treatment and prevention"; University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Birmingham Headache Centre, "Medication Overuse Headache information" (issued June 2026).
